summary: Defines the geo URI scheme for naming a physical location in two or three dimensions, in a compact and human-readable way. The default coordinate system is WGS-84. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a short way to write where something is on Earth, as a web-style address made of coordinates.

questions: what is the u parameter in geo uri
subtitle: A short, human-readable way to write a point on Earth as a URI, such as geo:13.4125,103.8667.

tldr.problem: Protocols and data formats each had their own way to attach a location, with no compact, protocol-independent way to refer to a geographic point.
tldr.mechanism: The geo URI scheme writes latitude, longitude and an optional altitude as comma-separated numbers, with optional crs and u parameters, using WGS-84 by default.
tldr.outcome: Any protocol or format that can carry a URI can now point at a physical place, and the RFC fixes how such URIs are compared and checked for validity.

today: RFC 5870 is a Proposed Standard from June 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the geo URI scheme.

sections.title: Why a geo URI
sections.content:
Many protocols and data formats add location by inventing their own latitude and longitude attributes. RFC 5870 defines the geo URI scheme instead, a compact, simple, human-readable and protocol-independent way to identify a physical location. The goal is that getting at a location should be no harder than clicking a mailto: link. The default coordinate reference system is the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS-84), and an example is geo:13.4125,103.8667.

The scheme is deliberately focused on one thing, a single point in a well-known coordinate system. More complex geometries and civic addresses are out of scope. WGS-84 was chosen because GPS devices use it and many other formats do too, so converting needs no re-projection.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every app inventing its own way to say where something is, geo gives them one short, shared way to write it down.

sections.title: The URI Syntax
sections.content:
A geo URI is the scheme name geo, a colon, two or three comma-separated numbers and optional parameters. The first two numbers are coordinates a and b, and the third is optional. Numbers may have a leading minus sign and a decimal fraction, and -0 is the same as 0.

The crs and u parameters may each appear at most once. They MUST come before any other parameters, and crs MUST come first if both are used. Parameter names are case insensitive, with lowercase preferred. The comma between coordinates MUST NOT be percent-encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is just the word geo, a colon, and a few numbers separated by commas. Extra details go after semicolons.

sections.title: Coordinates in WGS-84
sections.content:
For WGS-84, the three numbers are latitude and longitude in decimal degrees and an optional altitude in meters. Latitudes range from -90 to 90 and longitudes from -180 to 180. Southern and Western hemispheres, and altitudes below the WGS-84 reference geoid, are negative. A URI outside those ranges MUST be considered invalid.

If the altitude is unknown, it and the comma before it MUST NOT be present. Unknown altitude MUST NOT be written as 0, and an altitude of 0 MUST NOT be mistaken for ground elevation, because altitudes are relative to the geoid rather than the surface. At the poles, longitude SHOULD be 0, though consumers MUST accept any longitude from -180 to 180.

The two-dimensional case matches EPSG code 4326 and the three-dimensional case matches EPSG code 4979. The number of digits MUST NOT be read as a sign of accuracy.
sections.plainLanguage: Latitude says how far north or south you are, longitude how far east or west, and altitude how high. If you do not know the height, you leave it out instead of guessing zero.

sections.title: The crs and u Parameters
sections.content:
The optional crs parameter names the coordinate reference system. If it is missing or says wgs84, the default WGS-84 applies. No other values are defined, though future documents may add them. Consumers MUST NOT ignore a crs they are given, and clients MUST NOT try to dereference a URI in a system they do not know, since the result would be bogus.

The optional u parameter is the uncertainty of the location in meters, and applies to all dimensions in the URI. It can be set to zero to mean an exact point, but zero uncertainty and absent uncertainty are never the same thing: absent means unknown or unspecified.
sections.plainLanguage: The crs part says which map system the numbers use. The u part says how fuzzy the spot is, like saying within 40 meters of here.

sections.title: Comparing geo URIs
sections.content:
Comparison checks whether two URI strings are equivalent, not whether the places are close. Two geo URIs are equal only if they use the same coordinate system, their coordinates and u are mathematically identical (so 43.10 equals 43.1), and their other parameters are equal. Parameter order does not matter. A URI without altitude never equals one with altitude.

Two WGS-84 special cases apply: at latitude 90 or -90 the longitude MUST be ignored (the poles), and longitude 180 equals -180 (the date line). For unknown parameters, two URIs are equal only if the same names appear and the values are bitwise identical after percent-decoding. Otherwise the comparison is undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: Two addresses count as the same if they name the same numbers, even if one writes a trailing zero. At the North Pole every direction is the same spot.

sections.title: Use Cases and GML Mappings
sections.content:
Non-normative examples show a plain URI such as geo:48.2010,16.3695,183, a web link with geo:48.198634,16.371648;crs=wgs84;u=40, and a 2-dimensional barcode on a flyer that a phone could decode and use to start navigation. A browser might open a map, or a GPS receiver might start navigation.

Section 7 also gives non-normative mappings to Geography Markup Language (GML) from RFC 5491. Depending on the number of coordinates and whether u is present and non-zero, a geo URI maps to a GML Point, Circle or Sphere. A GML point always converts to a URI without an uncertainty parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: You could print a geo address as a square barcode on a flyer. A phone scans it and shows the way there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because a geo URI names a physical place, not a network resource, most general URI security considerations do not apply. Two issues remain. First, the syntax allows URIs that do not identify a valid place, such as geo:94,0. Applications MUST NOT use such URIs and SHOULD warn the user.

Second, a geo URI alone is just an opaque reference to a place. If it is used in a context where it identifies the location of a Target, it becomes part of a Location Object and is subject to the GEOPRIV rules, so the privacy requirements of RFC 3693 MUST be met.
sections.plainLanguage: A made-up place like north of the North Pole should not be trusted. And if the place tells where a person is, their privacy must be protected.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers the permanent geo scheme in the IETF part of the URI tree. It creates a "'geo' URI Parameters" registry with initial entries crs (Predefined) and u (Constrained), under the "Specification Required" policy. It also creates a sub-registry for crs values, with wgs84 as the initial entry, which needs both "Specification Required" and "IESG Approval".
sections.plainLanguage: A public list records the allowed extras, so two people do not invent different meanings for the same word.

viz.caption: GEO URI ABNF (EXCERPT FROM RFC 5870, SECTION 3.3)

data.title: geo URI syntax
data.code:
geo-URI       = geo-scheme ":" geo-path
geo-scheme    = "geo"
geo-path      = coordinates p
coordinates   = coord-a "," coord-b [ "," coord-c ]

p             = [ crsp ] [ uncp ] *parameter
crsp          = ";crs=" crslabel
crslabel      = "wgs84" / labeltext
uncp          = ";u=" uval
uval          = pnum

viz.caption: GEO URI TO GML MAPPING (RFC 5870, SECTION 7)

items.title: Numbers, not strings
items.text: 43.10 and 43.1 are the same number, so they compare equal.

items.title: Poles
items.text: At latitude 90 or -90, longitude is ignored.

items.title: Altitude
items.text: A URI with no altitude never equals one with altitude.
